Japan's Regions.text: The world map is one true-scale map of central and western Japan, from northern Kyushu east along the Seto Inland Sea and the Kansai cities, across the Japanese Alps and the Tokai coast to Tokyo, the Boso Peninsula and the mountains of Niigata and Fukushima. Every square on it is about 60 kilometers across, so the gaps between places on the map are the real distances, and every square that is not part of the story is real Japanese country, town or sea, there to travel through. Musutafu, a Shizuoka city on Suruga Bay at the root of the Izu Peninsula, lies below U.A. Campus, the forested hill country on Mount Fuji's eastern foothills that holds U.A. Academy's walled grounds; its station is a shinkansen stop 45 minutes from Tokyo. South of it run Tartarus Coast, the Izu Peninsula's tip with the Tartarus Transfer Port, and Tartarus Waters, the open Pacific among the Izu Islands where the prison Tartarus stands alone on its island. Greater Tokyo, about 100 kilometers northeast of Musutafu, is the capital and the heart of the hero business: Tokyo Station, the Hero Public Safety Commission Headquarters, the agencies of Endeavor and Best Jeanist, avenues of hero billboards, and, about 30 kilometers north of the center, Hosu, a dense commuter city with elevated railways, crowded back alleys and too few heroes. Kamino and Yokohama, the bay shore southwest of the capital, pairs Yokohama's working port and Chinatown with Kamino Ward, a tired old ward of shuttered shops and idle warehouses, and Takoba Municipal Stadium, a venue for the Commission's license exam. Northwest of Tokyo, about 100 kilometers out in the mountains, lie Deika, a prosperous company town built around the support maker Detnerat below Gunga Mountain, and Jaku, a quieter basin city with the district's largest hospital. The Mountain Training Lands in the Kiso valley of the Japanese Alps, three to four hours by bus from Musutafu, are the private forest of the Wild Wild Pussycats, where U.A. holds its summer training camps. Osaka North and Osaka South, two hours west of Musutafu by shinkansen to Shin-Osaka Station, are Osaka and its neighbors Kyoto and Nara: canals, neon, covered arcades, the agencies of Fat Gum and Sir Nighteye, and one old yakuza compound. Kyushu, at the western end of the map, is Fukuoka and Hakata on the island's north coast, home of the Hawks Hero Agency, about 4.5 hours from Musutafu by shinkansen. Between them the map holds the real country: the Hokuriku coast and the Noto Peninsula on the Sea of Japan, the Japanese Alps and the volcanoes of Nagano and Gunma, Nagoya and the Tokai cities along the Pacific, the castle towns and ports of the Seto Inland Sea, Shikoku's mountains and capes, the San'in coast and the Oki Islands, and the seas around them. Getting between the story's cities still means a train, a bus, a ferry or a plane, and the trip takes the real time.
